title: Fire the critic, taste the batch
allegory: GRPO is a chef who fires the food critic: instead of paying someone to predict how good a dish from each recipe ought to be, she cooks a small batch from the same recipe, has every dish scored, and learns from how each one did against the batch's own average.
map: a batch of dishes cooked from the same card
a group of completions sampled for that prompt
the judge's score for each finished dish
the sequence-level reward, e.g. a verifier on the final answer
beating the batch average, in units of how much the batch varied
the advantage (r − mean(r)) / std(r), taken within the group
the food critic she stops paying
PPO's value head: a second network about as big as the policy

cap.1: Tuning a language model with PPO means carrying a second network, the critic, about as big as the model itself. You already carry a frozen copy too.
cap.2: PPO's advantage needs a baseline, and PPO learns it: a value head with its own loss. For an LLM that critic is comparable in size to the policy, on top of the frozen reference kept for the KL penalty.
cap.3: PPO estimates A_t with GAE over a learned V(s). For LLM tuning V is roughly policy-sized and needs its own loss, beside π_ref held for the KL term. DeepSeekMath (DeepSeek-AI, 2024) dropped it.

cap.1: So fire the critic. For each recipe, cook a small batch, get every dish scored, and learn from how each one did against the batch's own average.
cap.2: For each prompt, sample a group of completions and score each finished one. The group's mean reward replaces the critic's prediction as the baseline. Better than its siblings counts as better.
cap.3: The baseline becomes empirical and per-prompt: the group mean estimates that prompt's expected reward with no parameters, its noise shrinking as the group grows. Rollout cost rises instead.

cap.1: A dish's push is its score minus the batch average, divided by how much the batch varied. Scores 3, 7, 5, 9 average 6: the 9 goes up, the 3 goes down.
cap.2: In the exercise you override rollout_phase to sample a group per prompt, then take mean and std within each prompt's group, never across the batch. That z-score is the advantage.
cap.3: A_i = (r_i − mean(r)) / std(r) over the G samples of one prompt. No GAE, no value loss, no critic parameters: two substitutions relative to PPO, and only two.

chapters.name: Scores become pushes
chapters.title: Four answers to one prompt: score, then push

cap.1: The four scores become pushes: the 9 gets the biggest push up, the 3 the biggest push down. Every word of an answer shares that answer's single push.
cap.2: Rewards are per sequence, so each completion's one advantage is broadcast to every generated token in it. A good answer's filler gets the same credit as its key step.
cap.3: Here std is the population value √5; torch.std defaults to the sample version, scaling every A by √((G−1)/G). Broadcasting gives no within-sequence credit: fine for a final-answer verifier, weak otherwise.

chapters.name: Only compare siblings

left.title: normalised across the batch
lines: easy question: every answer looks great
hard question: every answer looks bad
you reward the question, not the answer

chapters.verdict: Compare each answer only with answers to the same question.

cap.1: Easy recipes score high whatever you do. Average over every dish in the kitchen and you praise the easy recipe, not the good cooking. Compare within each batch.
cap.2: Normalising across the whole batch quietly turns 'this prompt is easier than that one' back into training signal. Test it: two prompts together must give the same advantages as each alone.
cap.3: Batch-level normalisation mixes between-prompt variance into A, rewarding prompt difficulty, not answer quality. Assert the reduction axis: rewards reshaped to (n_prompts, G), stats over dim=-1.

cap.1: If every dish in a batch burns, or every one is perfect, none beats the average and that recipe teaches nothing. As the cook improves, more recipes go quiet.
cap.2: When every completion in a group gets the same reward, all advantages are zero and the prompt adds no gradient. Log the fraction of zero-variance groups each phase: that's your real batch size.
cap.3: Uniform groups give r − mean(r) = 0 and std = 0, and a bare epsilon turns float noise into zeros or wild values. Floor it (std + 1e-4), skip those groups, mix prompt difficulty, raise G.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The standard recipe for RL on reasoning models
Best where answers can be checked: maths, code
PPO's clip and KL leash, minus the critic

cap.1: Many reasoning models learn from graded answers this way. What they get steered towards is whatever beats their own other attempts, as the grader sees it.
cap.2: GRPO fits verifiable rewards: maths answers, unit tests. It keeps PPO's clipped ratio and the KL penalty to a frozen reference; only the baseline changed. The grader defines 'better'.
cap.3: DeepSeekMath 7B: 51.7% on MATH with no tools or voting, 60.9% with self-consistency over 64 samples. To steer a GRPO-trained model, steer its reward: the group only ranks siblings.

coda.title: Eight answers to one maths question, each marked right (1) or wrong (0): each answer's push

params.label: divide by the spread (0 off, 1 on)

readouts.label: push on each right answer
readouts.f: k == 0 ? 'no right answers' : ((1 - k/8)/(s > 0.5 ? sqrt(k/8*(1 - k/8)) + 1e-4 : 1)).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: push on each wrong answer
readouts.f: k == 8 ? 'no wrong answers' : ((0 - k/8)/(s > 0.5 ? sqrt(k/8*(1 - k/8)) + 1e-4 : 1)).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: does this question teach anything?
readouts.f: k == 0 || k == 8 ? 'no: every answer scored the same' : 'yes'

caption.1: Slide how many of the eight answers are right. When only one is right, watch its push tower over the rest. Then try 0 or 8: nothing moves at all.
caption.2: A lone right answer gets a big boost; a lone wrong one a big penalty. Switch the spread off and every push shrinks, lopsided groups most. At 0 or 8 right, every push is zero.
caption.3: With 0/1 marks and p = k/G: A_right = √((1−p)/p), A_wrong = −√(p/(1−p)) (population std). Every mixed group gets Σ A² = G, so each informative question has equal say; uniform groups get none.

where_else: REINFORCE with a baseline: GRPO's group mean is a baseline you measure instead of learn
PPO: the same clipped ratio and KL leash, with a learned critic in place of the group
Verifiable-reward training on code and maths: unit tests and answer checkers as the judge
Marking on a curve: a score means little until it sits next to others who sat the same paper

hamming.what: PPO without a critic: sample a group of answers to each prompt, score them, and use each answer's reward against its group's mean, scaled by the group's spread, as its advantage.
hamming.when: When rewards can be checked, like maths answers or unit tests, and you can't afford a policy-sized critic in memory.
hamming.why: Better than its siblings on the same question is a perfectly good definition of better, it costs no network, and it became the standard recipe for RL on reasoning models.

object.title: The teaching table
object.subtitle: Each plinth is one question; its height is the chance its group of answers disagrees, so it teaches something.

knobs.label: How good the model has got

cap.1: Each plinth is a question; its height is the chance a group of answers to it disagrees, so it teaches something. Hard questions left, easy ones right.
cap.2: Height is 1 − pᴳ − (1 − p)ᴳ: the chance a group of G answers holds at least one right and one wrong, for a question the model solves with probability p.
cap.3: With 0/1 rewards a group has nonzero advantages only if it is mixed. P(mixed) = 1 − pᴳ − (1 − p)ᴳ for independent samples; the rows are G = 2, 4, 8, 16.

cap.1: Questions solved about half the time nearly always teach. Ones nearly always missed, or nearly always solved, often come back silent, worst with small groups.
cap.2: At p = 0.5 even a pair disagrees half the time, and a group of 16 almost always does. Near p = 0 or 1, small groups are usually uniform and add zero gradient.
cap.3: P(uniform) = pᴳ + (1 − p)ᴳ is smallest at p = 0.5 for every G ≥ 2, where it falls as 2^(1−G); near the extremes it stays close to 1 unless G is large compared with 1/p or 1/(1 − p).

cap.1: Now the model has improved. Most questions come back all right, the plinths sink, and training stalls just when it was going well.
cap.2: As the policy gets good, more groups are uniformly correct: advantages vanish, the loss is tiny and the effective batch shrinks. That's the stall: loss tiny, reward flat.
cap.3: Shifting every question's logit up by 3 pushes most p towards 1, so the fraction of informative groups collapses and the gradient comes from a shrinking, noisy subset of prompts.

cap.1: From the side: the back row, groups of 16, holds up best. With more tries a rare wrong answer is likelier to show up, and it teaches a lot.
cap.2: Raising the group size is one fix: a mixed outcome becomes more likely on easy and hard questions alike. It costs more rollouts per prompt.
cap.3: For p near 1, P(mixed) ≈ 1 − pᴳ grows with G. Each extra sample buys signal with generation compute: the trade GRPO makes instead of holding a critic in memory.

cap.1: The other fix: curate. Swap in questions pitched where the model is now, solved about half the time, and the table stands tall again.
cap.2: Curate or resample prompts so groups are mixed rather than uniformly hard or uniformly easy. The curate knob re-centres the question pool on the model's current skill.
cap.3: Prompt selection keeps p away from 0 and 1, maximising informative groups per rollout; skipping zero-variance groups then wastes nothing on float noise.

predict.q: All eight answers to a question are marked right. What does that question add to the update?

options.t: A strong push towards those answers

predict.why: Every reward equals the group mean, so r − mean(r) = 0 for every answer. There is no sibling to beat.

predict.q: You normalise advantages across the whole batch instead of within each group. What sneaks into the signal?

options.t: Which questions are easy, not which answers are good
Nothing: the advantages come out the same

predict.why: Across the batch, every answer to an easy question looks above average. Within its group, an answer only races its siblings.

predict.q: One of eight answers is right. How does its push compare with each wrong answer's?

options.t: About seven times bigger, in the other direction
The same size, just the other sign

predict.why: With 0/1 marks the pushes are 1 − p and −p before dividing by the spread; at p = 1/8 that is 7/8 against −1/8.

object.where: Anywhere a score only means something beside its siblings: marking on a curve per exam question, or ranking several attempts at the same task.
